passage:
Monday. Francis liked Samir's photo and, near midnight, sent "thinking of you 🙂". Samir smiled all through morning lectures. Then three days of nothing, until a meme arrived with no words.
Saturday. Samir noticed the pattern: warm bursts, never a plan. He wrote, "I'd like to actually meet this week. Would you?" Francis answered, "Ha, soon! Crazy busy right now."
Two weeks later. After another round of hearts and silence, Samir wrote, "I'm looking for someone who makes plans. I'll step back. Take care." His chest felt heavy, but he stopped checking his phone every hour, and on Sunday he went cycling with his friends.

qa.q: What did Francis send near midnight?
qa.a: Francis sent "thinking of you" with a smiling emoji.

qa.q: What did Samir feel on Monday morning, and what had changed by Saturday?
qa.a: He felt happy and hopeful and smiled all morning. By Saturday he saw that the warm messages never became plans, so he wanted a clear answer.

qa.q: Why was asking directly a good step for Samir?
qa.a: It gave Francis a chance to offer real plans and showed Samir what he was actually getting. When no plan came, he could step back instead of waiting for scraps.

qa.q: How might Francis see those messages?
qa.a: Francis may see them as friendly and casual rather than a promise, while Samir read them as hope. The vague "soon" shows Francis did not offer more.

grounding: Someone gives just enough attention to keep the protagonist hoping; he asks clearly and walks away when nothing is offered.

passage:
Naveen: hey stranger 👋 saw this song and thought of u
Anjali: haha nice. it's been 12 days since you replied to me
Naveen: been crazy busy. we should hang out sometime!!
Anjali: you said that last month too. and before your exams
Naveen: I mean it this time 😊
Anjali: Okay, being honest. I like you, and I'd like to actually date, not just get a song every two weeks. Are you interested in that?
Naveen: whoa, that's heavy. can't we just keep it chill?
Anjali: Chill for you means I wait by my phone.
Anjali: So I'll take that as a no, and that's okay. I'm going to stop waiting.
Naveen: wait you're mad?
Anjali: Not mad. Just done living on the odd message. Take care, Naveen.

qa.q: How many days had passed since Naveen last replied to Anjali?
qa.a: It had been 12 days since Naveen replied.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when asking Naveen the direct question?
qa.a: Anjali felt hopeful but tired and a little hurt, since the same 'we should hang out' promise had been made before and never kept.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Anjali's place after hearing 'can't we just keep it chill?'
qa.a: Treat it as a no, say so kindly, and stop waiting, as Anjali did, instead of holding on for the next song.

qa.q: How does Naveen seem to see the conversation?
qa.a: Naveen seems caught off guard and a bit defensive, calling a clear request 'heavy' and asking if Anjali is mad, because the loose attention suited Naveen.

grounding: Illustrates breadcrumbing through scattered friendly messages, and the wise move of asking plainly for what one wants and walking away when it is not offered.

passage: Every evening Ojas cycled past the sweet shop in the Karjat bazaar, because Tanuja sometimes sat on its step with her cousins. Some days she waved him over, laughed at his jokes and asked him to drop her at the bus stand. Other days she looked straight through him. Twice she promised to come to the temple fair with him, and twice she sent a last-minute message: 'Next time, pakka.' At the fair, his friend Bablu watched him check his phone again and said, 'You're living on crumbs, yaar.' The next evening Ojas asked her outright, on the step, whether she wanted to spend time with him properly. Tanuja shrugged and said she liked keeping things open. Ojas nodded, said that wasn't enough for him, and from then on took the long road home past the canal.

qa.q: Where did Tanuja sometimes sit in the evenings?
qa.a: Tanuja sat on the step of the sweet shop in the Karjat bazaar, with her cousins.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when Tanuja said she liked keeping things open?
qa.a: Ojas was disappointed and hurt, but also clearer: he had hoped for more and decided the little he was getting was not enough.

qa.q: Which step helped Ojas stop living on crumbs?
qa.a: Asking Tanuja outright what she wanted, accepting her answer, and changing his route home so he was no longer waiting at the shop.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see the arrangement?
qa.a: Tanuja seems comfortable with it, enjoying his attention and rides without committing, which is why she shrugs and prefers to keep things open.

grounding: Shows occasional warmth and broken promises keeping someone hoping, until he asks clearly and walks away when nothing more is offered.
